paras: The beating of a Pullman porter at Sterling, Georgia, took place on about October 21, 1903, when an unnamed Black sleeping-car porter on Southern Railway train No. 14 was beaten by George H. Smith, treasurer of the city of Brunswick, and then put off the train in the woods. He was accused of speaking insolently to a woman passenger bound for Spartanburg, South Carolina. Several South Carolina weeklies reprinted the story as a lesson in manners under headlines such as 'It Pays to be Polite.'

According to a Brunswick dispatch to the Atlanta News, the porter 'demanded, in an insolent manner, to see the passenger's transportation,' and when the woman asked him to repeat the question he did so 'in a more insulting way.' A second Brunswick dispatch said instead that he had spoken to her about transferring to another train and repeated it 'very insolently.' Neither account gives the porter's own version of the exchange.

Smith, who was riding on the train, then attacked the porter. The Atlanta News dispatch said Smith and 'a stranger' set upon him and that he was 'terribly beaten,' while the other dispatch said Smith alone 'gave him a thrashing.' According to the second dispatch, the porter appealed to the conductor, named there as Tengale (Temple in the Atlanta News version), but 'got little sympathy.'

The conductor ordered the porter off the train at Sterling, which the Atlanta News dispatch described as 'a town in the woods.' The second dispatch said the conductor stopped the train and 'hustled' him off in the woods without letting him change out of his uniform, and the first said he was not allowed to collect his baggage or travel further. Both dispatches said the porter came from Milwaukee, and the first said his name could not be learned in Brunswick.
No report of an arrest, charge or other action against Smith or the stranger was found in the coverage, and nothing further appears about the porter.

The Savannah Morning News carried the Atlanta News dispatch on October 23 under the headline 'For Insulting a Woman,' presenting the porter's insult as fact. The longer Brunswick special, which ran in the Yorkville Enquirer on October 27 and in the Bamberg Herald on October 29, was openly mocking: the porter was 'left there to meditate how much better it is for a Negro to be polite even if he is in the uniform of the Pullmans,' and was called 'the insolent darkey' and 'the Negro who was taught a lesson in manners.' The Sumter Watchman and Southron printed the same text on October 28 under 'Insolent Pullman Porter,' with a subhead stating that 'Passengers Put Him Off,' although its own text credited the conductor.

A condensed version titled 'It Pays to be Polite' appeared in the Manning Times and the Batesburg Advocate on October 28 and the Marlboro Democrat on October 30. Every report came from white papers in Georgia and South Carolina and framed the beating as deserved, and no coverage of the incident in the Black press was found.
The accounts differ on the number of attackers, the conductor's name, and the date, which the dated Brunswick special puts on Wednesday, October 21, and the condensed version on Thursday.

reader.title: Beating of a Pullman porter at Sterling, Georgia
bases: A Black Pullman porter was beaten on a train by one or two white passengers and then put off the train in the woods, with no threat to kill reported (A1, A2); the assailants were individuals rather than a crowd, so this is a mob assault only in the loose sense.

Two differently worded dispatches from Brunswick, one via the Atlanta News (A1) and one a 'special' (A2, A6), agree that George H. Smith beat the porter and that he was put off train No. 14, though both reflect the assailants' and conductor's side.

accounts.label: Atlanta News dispatch from Brunswick
accounts.gist: The porter insolently demanded to see a woman's ticket; Smith and a stranger 'terribly beat' him and Conductor Temple ordered him off at Sterling without his baggage.

accounts.label: Brunswick special (South Carolina reprints)
accounts.gist: The porter spoke insolently to a woman about changing trains; Smith alone thrashed him, and Conductor Tengale stopped the train and put him off in the woods without letting him change his uniform.

accounts.label: Shortened version
accounts.gist: A condensed text dating the event to Thursday near Brunswick, ending simply 'He was then put off the train.'

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed the item 'For Insulting a Woman' and gave only the passengers' version of the porter's conduct.

The Brunswick special said he was left 'to meditate how much better it is for a Negro to be polite' and called him 'the insolent darkey'; headlines read 'Insolent Pullman Porter' and 'It Pays to be Polite'.

conflicts.note: Both are Brunswick dispatches; neither is clearly better evidence.
